kurals.tamil:
கற்க கசடறக் கற்பவை கற்றபின்
நிற்க அதற்குத் தக.
kurals.transliteration:
Karka kasadarak karpavai katrapin
Nirka adharkuth thaga.
kurals.meaning: Learn what is worth learning, and learn it thoroughly, without flaw or gap. Then, once you have learned it, live in a way that matches what you have learned.
kurals.elementary: Imagine learning all the rules of football perfectly but then cheating in the game. That would make the learning pointless. This kural says two things: learn good things properly, then actually live by them.
kurals.university: The chapter on Kalvi opens with a two-step command. The first is கற்க கசடற: learn so that no flaw (kasadu) is left, which traditional commentators such as Parimelazhagar read as choosing the right texts and also removing one's own mental faults through study. The second is நிற்க அதற்குத் தக: stand, or remain, in conduct fitting to that learning. The verb நிற்க (to stand) is significant, because it pictures learning as a place one lives in and not only a set of facts one holds. Because the chapter sits in the Porul section, just after the chapter on kingship, this is also advice to rulers: a king's learning is shown in how he governs, not in how much he can recite. The same link between knowing and doing appears across many traditions, from the Epistle of James to the Stoic Epictetus.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the teacher's farewell address to graduating students in the Taittiriya Upanishad, the student is told to speak the truth, practise dharma, and never neglect study (svadhyaya).
hinduism.explanation: This is a traditional convocation charge. When formal study ends, the teacher says learning must now become right conduct and must also continue as lifelong self-study.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats finishing one's studies as the start of living by them. Both parts are there: study faithfully, then act accordingly.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage. It pairs study with dharmic conduct, but it is a list of duties rather than a direct statement that conduct must match learning.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.”
christianity.explanation: James warns believers that hearing or knowing God's teaching is not enough. Anyone who does not act on it is fooling themselves.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the second half of the Kural: once you have learned, stand by it in action.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on BibleGateway (KJV). A strong match for the idea that learning must turn into conduct.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Greatly hateful in the sight of Allāh is that you say what you do not do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an condemns a gap between what people profess and what they practise. Knowing and saying the right thing without doing it is called hateful to God.
islam.tie_back: It gives the negative side of the Kural's command. Once you know what is right, your conduct has to match it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the Quran.com API (Saheeh International). The verse is about speech versus action, which is close to learning versus conduct.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone whose deeds exceed his wisdom, his wisdom is enduring, but anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, his wisdom is not enduring.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa teaches that learning lasts only when it is rooted in and outweighed by action. Wisdom without deeds withers away.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost a Jewish twin of the Kural: learning is real only when conduct stands in line with it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria (Mishnah Yomit, Dr. Joshua Kulp). A very close thematic match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares someone who knows many texts but does not practise them to a hired cowherd. He counts cattle that are not his own and never gets their milk.
buddhism.tie_back: Same point as the Kural: learning that is not lived gives nothing to the learner.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. A near one-to-one match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Athena is at once the goddess of wisdom (metis) and the patron of practical crafts such as weaving, shipbuilding and strategy. In Greek myth her wisdom always shows itself in skilled action.
greek_mythology.explanation: Athena's wisdom is never idle. It appears in finished work, sound counsel and well-fought battles.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Loosely parallel: Greek myth pictures true wisdom as knowledge expressed in deeds, as the Kural asks.
greek_mythology.source: General Greek mythology (Homeric Hymn 28 to Athena; Hesiod, Theogony 886–900 on Metis)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak match. Greek myth has no clear story commanding people to live by their learning. Athena's joining of wisdom and craft is the closest available parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never call yourself a philosopher, nor talk a great deal among the unlearned about theorems, but act conformably to them.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells his students that philosophy is proven by behaviour, not by talk. At a dinner party, do not lecture on how people should eat. Simply eat as one should.
philosophy.tie_back: This echoes the Kural's second line, where learning must be shown by standing in conduct that fits it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Wording confirmed against multiple online editions of the Carter/Higginson translation. A strong thematic match.

kurals.tamil:
எண்ணென்ப ஏனை எழுத்தென்ப இவ்விரண்டும்
கண்ணென்ப வாழும் உயிர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ennenba enai ezhuthenba ivvirandum
Kannenba vaazhum uyirkku.
kurals.meaning: What are called numbers, and the other thing called letters: the wise say these two are the eyes of every living person.
kurals.elementary: You have two eyes to see the world. Valluvar says your mind also has two eyes: numbers and letters. Maths and reading let you understand things you could never see without them.
kurals.university: This kural reduces the whole of learning to two basic disciplines, எண் (en, number and calculation) and எழுத்து (ezhuthu, letters and literacy), and calls them the two eyes of human life. Commentators widened the terms. Parimelazhagar took en to cover arithmetic and the sciences such as astronomy, and ezhuthu to cover grammar and literature. The modern commentator Solomon Pappaiah even glosses them as science and the arts. The repeated என்ப ('they say') presents this as settled wisdom, not personal opinion. The image of eyes prepares for the next kural, where lacking learning is compared to having sores instead of eyes. Remarkably, Aeschylus' Prometheus names the very same pair, numbers and the combining of letters, as the founding gifts of civilization.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Mundaka Upanishad teaches that two kinds of knowledge must be known, the higher (para) and the lower (apara). The lower includes the four Vedas together with phonetics, grammar, etymology, metre, ritual and astronomy.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad sorts all learning into a twofold scheme. The 'lower' disciplines, which include the sciences of letters (phonetics and grammar) and of calculation (astronomy), are the tools that come before and serve the higher knowledge.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats learning as a pair of essential faculties. Its lower knowledge includes exactly the letter-based and number-based sciences that Valluvar calls the two eyes.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Partial match. Both passages speak of two kinds of knowledge, but the Upanishad's pair is lower versus higher, not numbers versus letters. Paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes God's written word as the light that lets him see where he is walking.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's image of learning as eyes, the organs of sight, matches the Psalm's image of the written word as light for the path.
christianity._accuracy_note: Metaphorical match only. It shares the sight and illumination image but refers to scripture, not numeracy and literacy.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who taught by the pen - Taught man that which he knew not.”
islam.explanation: In the first verses revealed to the Prophet, God is praised as the One who taught humanity through the pen, meaning through writing. Literacy is presented as a divine gift that opens up knowledge.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an honours ezhuthu, letters and writing, as the channel by which people come to know what they did not know. This mirrors the Kural's claim that letters are an eye of life.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the Quran.com API. A strong match for 'letters'. Numbers are not mentioned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The calculation of the equinoxes and gematria are the desserts of wisdom.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer Hisma names astronomical calculation and gematria (the numerical values of letters) as the delightful extras that round out Torah learning.
judaism.tie_back: Here numbers and letters meet, since gematria is literally letters read as numbers. The Mishnah treats both as part of complete wisdom, though as supplements rather than 'eyes'.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria. It links numbers and letters to wisdom, but calls them 'desserts', which is less central than the Kural's 'eyes'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To have much learning, to be skillful in handicraft, well-trained in discipline, and to be of good speech — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Discourse on Blessings, the Buddha lists extensive learning (bahusacca) and practical skill (sippa) among the highest blessings of a good life.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats basic learning and skills as essential to living well, not as optional ornaments.
buddhism.source: Mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. It praises learning in general. It does not name numbers and letters specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Aye, and numbers, too, chiefest of sciences, I invented for them, and the combining of letters, creative mother of the Muses' arts, wherewith to hold all things in memory.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Chained to his rock, the Titan Prometheus lists the gifts he gave to helpless early humans. Numbers and writing come near the top as the foundations of all other arts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An exact pairing: Aeschylus names numbers and letters as the twin gifts that made human life truly human, just as Valluvar calls them life's two eyes.
greek_mythology.source: Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 459–461 (trans. H. W. Smyth)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Smyth (Loeb 1927) wording confirmed against Wikisource and Theoi editions. A striking, near-exact parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Galileo writes that philosophy is written in the great book of the universe. That book cannot be understood unless one first learns its language and reads its letters, and it is written in the language of mathematics.
philosophy.explanation: For Galileo, reading and mathematics together are the only way to 'see' nature. Without them a person wanders as if in a dark labyrinth.
philosophy.tie_back: This parallels the Kural closely: letters and numbers are the faculties through which reality becomes visible.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage. Translations vary, so it is not given as a verbatim quote. The 'letters plus mathematics as the means of sight' theme is a strong match.

kurals.tamil:
கண்ணுடையர் என்பவர் கற்றோர் முகத்திரண்டு
புண்ணுடையர் கல்லா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kannudaiyar enbavar katror mugaththirandu
Punnudaiyar kallaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Only the learned can truly be said to have eyes. Those without learning merely carry two sores on their face.
kurals.elementary: Two holes in your face are not the same as seeing. If you never learn anything, your eyes look at the world but understand nothing. Valluvar says a person who learns has real eyes.
kurals.university: Continuing the eye metaphor of Kural 392, Valluvar reaches one of the harshest images in the chapter. The unlearned person's eyes are புண் (pun), wounds or sores: openings in the face that do nothing and may even be painful. The contrast rests on the difference between physical sight and understanding. Kalaignar's commentary draws the corollary that a learned person without physical sight still 'has eyes', while an unlearned person with sight does not. The rhetoric is deliberately provocative. It belongs to a statecraft section meant to push kings and citizens toward education, and the following chapter, Kallaamai (Ignorance), develops the same harshness. Similar contrasts between seeing eyes and a seeing mind run through the Gospels, the Qur'an and Plato.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A famous verse of Bhartrhari's Nitishataka says that a person without literature, music and the arts is a beast in plain sight, only lacking a tail and horns.
hinduism.explanation: Bhartrhari, the Sanskrit poet-grammarian, uses shock imagery to insist that culture and learning are what make someone fully human.
hinduism.tie_back: Same rhetorical strategy as the Kural: the unlearned person keeps an outwardly human form but lacks what that form is for, just as a face may carry 'sores' instead of eyes.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Sanskrit verse. Verse numbering varies by recension. The provocative 'the unlearned lack their true human faculty' theme is a strong match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus describes people whose eyes work perfectly but who still fail to perceive the truth in front of them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it separates having eyes from truly seeing. Understanding is what turns sight into vision.
christianity._accuracy_note: Standard KJV text. The 'eyes that do not see' theme is a close match, though the Gospel is about spiritual receptivity rather than education.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says that true blindness is in the heart and mind that fail to understand, not in the physical eyes.
islam.tie_back: This strongly parallels the Kural: physical eyes do not count as sight without inner understanding.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the Quran.com API. The inner-versus-outer sight contrast is nearly identical to the Kural's.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A brute is not sin-fearing, nor is an ignorant person pious.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel teaches that a person with no learning at all (bur, 'empty field') cannot even reach basic moral seriousness, and an unlettered person cannot be truly pious.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees ignorance as a real deficiency in the person, not a neutral state. Its focus is on piety rather than 'sight'.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria. Thematically related (ignorance as a defect) but without the eye imagery.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man of little learning grows old like a bull. He grows only in bulk, but, his wisdom does not grow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares an unlearned person to an ox that gets bigger with age but never gets wiser.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it uses a blunt image to show that a body without learning is a diminished life.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. The same 'harsh image for the unlearned' strategy, with an ox image instead of eye imagery.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles' Oedipus the King, the blind prophet Tiresias sees the truth, while Oedipus, with perfect eyesight, is blind to who he is. When Oedipus finally understands, he puts out his own eyes.
greek_mythology.explanation: The tragedy is built on the reversal of sight and insight. The man with eyes cannot see, and the eyeless seer knows everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This closely parallels the Kural. Eyes without understanding are useless or even wounds, and understanding is the real sight. Oedipus literally turns his eyes into wounds.
greek_mythology.source: Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus (esp. the Tiresias scene, lines 300–462, and the self-blinding)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased summary of the plot. The sight-versus-insight theme is a strong match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's Allegory of the Cave, prisoners watch shadows on a wall and take them for reality. Education is the painful turning of the soul toward the light, so that it finally sees what is real.
philosophy.explanation: Plato defines education not as putting sight into blind eyes but as turning the soul's existing 'eye' toward the truth.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Plato holds that the uneducated have eyes that do not truly see. Learning is what makes vision real.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Plato's 'eye of the soul' image directly parallels the Kural's 'eyes of the learned'.

kurals.tamil:
உவப்பத் தலைக்கூடி உள்ளப் பிரிதல்
அனைத்தே புலவர் தொழில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uvappath thalaikkoodi ullap piridhal
Anaiththe pulavar thozhil.
kurals.meaning: The mark of the learned is this: people rejoice when they meet them, and when they part, people keep thinking of them and long to meet again.
kurals.elementary: Think of a teacher or grandparent whose stories you love. When they come, you are happy. When they leave, you wish they could stay longer. Valluvar says that is how learned people make everyone feel.
kurals.university: Here Valluvar moves from the value of learning to its social effect. The புலவர் (pulavar, the learned or poet-scholar) is defined by an experience they create in others: உவப்ப, gladness at meeting, and உள்ளப் பிரிதல், parting in a way that leaves people thinking of them. The word தொழில் (thozhil, occupation or characteristic work) suggests that bringing joy through conversation is the scholar's real 'profession'. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan gloss the second half as others wondering when they will see such a person again. The kural implicitly contrasts true learning, which is generous and delightful, with pedantry that makes people glad to leave. Greek tradition offers vivid parallels, from Odysseus spellbinding the Phaeacians to Alcibiades' account of being enchanted by Socrates' words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Bhaja Govindam, Adi Shankaracharya teaches that the company of the good (satsanga) leads to non-attachment, then freedom from delusion, then steadiness of mind, and finally liberation.
hinduism.explanation: The tradition of satsang holds that simply being in the company of wise people transforms and uplifts the listener.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats time with the learned as a treasured, transforming experience. Shankara stresses spiritual effect rather than delight and longing.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. It praises the company of the wise, but does not describe joy at meeting or longing at parting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs describes how the meeting of wise minds leaves each person brighter and sharper.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes the benefit of meeting a wise person. The Proverb's emphasis is mutual improvement, while the Kural's is delight and longing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Standard KJV text. A moderate match: it concerns the benefit of good company, not the emotions of meeting and parting.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of a good pious companion and an evil one is that of a person carrying musk and another blowing a pair of bellows.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a good companion to a perfume seller. Even if you buy nothing, you leave carrying a pleasant fragrance.
islam.tie_back: The musk image matches the Kural well: time with a good, learned person leaves something pleasant that stays with you after you part.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sunnah.com. The 'lingering fragrance' is a good parallel to the lingering longing, though the hadith is about good companions in general rather than scholars.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If two sit together and there are words of Torah [spoken] between them, then the Shekhinah abides among them.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradion teaches that when people meet and share words of learning, the Divine Presence rests among them.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes a learned meeting a blessed, uplifting event. It focuses on sacred presence rather than personal delight.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria. It shows the elevated quality of learned conversation. The longing-at-parting element is absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To be patient and obedient, to associate with monks and to have religious discussions on due occasions — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Mangala Sutta counts meeting and discussing the Dhamma with learned, disciplined people among life's highest blessings.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats meeting the learned as a real joy and blessing.
buddhism.source: Mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. A general parallel about the blessing of learned company.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus pauses in telling his adventures at the Phaeacian court, his audience sits spellbound in silence. King Alcinous begs him to go on, saying they would listen until dawn.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus' learning, gained through long travel and hardship, makes his company so delightful that his hosts cannot bear to let him stop.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This fits the Kural closely: the listeners rejoice in his company and do not want it to end.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the 'intermezzo' in Book 11. A strong match for joyful meeting and reluctance to part.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's Symposium, Alcibiades says that when Socrates speaks, listeners are overwhelmed and enchanted. He compares Socrates to the satyr Marsyas, whose music held everyone spellbound, except that Socrates does it with bare words.
philosophy.explanation: Alcibiades testifies that Socrates' conversation stays in the soul long after it ends and keeps drawing him back.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's pulavar, Socrates makes others glad to meet him and unable to forget him afterward.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A vivid match for the enchanting effect of a learned person's company, though Alcibiades' feelings are also ambivalent.

kurals.tamil:
உடையார்முன் இல்லார்போல் ஏக்கற்றுங் கற்றார்
கடையரே கல்லா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Udaiyaarmun illaarpol ekkatrum katraar
Kadaiyare kallaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who humbly stand before their teachers, eager as the poor before the rich, and so gain learning, are truly superior. Those who will not stoop to learn are the lowest of all.
kurals.elementary: A hungry child waits eagerly for food. A good student waits just as eagerly to learn from a teacher, and is not too proud to ask. The kural says being too proud to learn is what really makes you low.
kurals.university: The kural draws on a social image any reader would recognize: the needy person standing anxiously (ஏக்கற்று) before the wealthy. It applies that image to the student before the teacher. What looks like humiliation is really the road to greatness, since those who learn this way are the truly elevated (கற்றார்), while those who refuse to learn are கடையர், the lowest. Solomon Pappaiah reads the second line as condemning those who are ashamed to stand and learn, which makes pride the real barrier to education. The inversion of rank is typical of Valluvar: outward humility produces inner eminence. Many traditions make the same point, from the Gita's call to approach a teacher with submission (echoed in the Sanskrit maxim vidyā dadāti vinayam, 'learning gives humility') to the Mishnah's warning that the shy or ashamed cannot learn.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just try to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him submissively and render service unto him. The self-realized souls can impart knowledge unto you because they have seen the truth.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that real knowledge is gained by approaching a teacher with humility (pranipata), sincere questioning and service.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-exact match to the Kural's picture of the student standing humbly before the teacher as a precondition for learning.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Wording confirmed via vedabase.io and other search results. Humble approach to a teacher is the direct theme.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs teaches that those who welcome instruction grow in knowledge, while those too proud to be corrected sink to the level of beasts.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks the teachable above the proud and unteachable, whom it calls 'brutish', much as the Kural calls them the lowest.
christianity._accuracy_note: Standard KJV text. It shares the teachable-versus-proud ranking, without the rich-and-poor image.

islam.quote_or_event: “Moses said to him, “May I follow you on [the condition] that you teach me from what you have been taught of sound judgement?””
islam.explanation: Even the prophet Moses humbly asks the mysterious servant of God (traditionally al-Khidr) to be allowed to follow him as a student.
islam.tie_back: A strong match for the Kural's first line: even the greatest must stand as seekers before those who know more.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the Quran.com API. A clear narrative example of humble discipleship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ben Zoma said: Who is wise? He who learns from every man.”
judaism.explanation: True wisdom, Ben Zoma teaches, belongs to the person humble enough to learn from anyone at all. Elsewhere in Avot (2:5), Hillel warns that 'a timid person [cannot] learn', meaning one ashamed to ask questions.
judaism.tie_back: Both teachings match the Kural: wisdom belongs to those who humbly seek it, and pride or shame keeps people ignorant.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria. Together the two passages closely match both lines of the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges disciples to follow a wise teacher eagerly, as someone would follow a person who knew where treasure was buried.
buddhism.tie_back: The treasure-seeker image mirrors the Kural's 'poor before the rich'. The learner approaches the teacher as the needy approach wealth.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. The wealth imagery for the teacher is a notable parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Young Telemachus, sent to seek news from old King Nestor, confesses he feels ashamed and inexperienced about questioning an elder. Athena, disguised as Mentor, tells him to take courage and ask.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess of wisdom herself pushes the young man past his shyness so that he can learn from an experienced elder.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This fits the Kural closely. The learner must humbly approach the one who knows, and shame about asking is the obstacle to overcome.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. The 'shy student urged to approach the elder' scene closely matches the Kural's theme.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates explains that the Delphic oracle called him wisest only because, unlike others, he knew that he did not know. His wisdom began with admitting his own poverty of knowledge.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, recognizing one's ignorance, the stance of the 'poor' before knowledge, is the starting point of all real learning.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes humble awareness of one's own need the basis of true superiority in learning.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. It shares the humility-as-the-basis-of-wisdom theme but has no teacher-student image.

kurals.tamil:
தொட்டனைத் தூறும் மணற்கேணி மாந்தர்க்குக்
கற்றனைத் தூறும் அறிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thottanaith thoorum manarkeni maandharkkuk
Katranaith thoorum arivu.
kurals.meaning: A well dug in sandy ground gives water in proportion to how deep it is dug. In the same way, understanding wells up in a person in proportion to how much they have learned.
kurals.elementary: When you dig a hole at the beach, water starts to seep in, and the deeper you dig, the more water comes. Your mind works the same way: the more you learn, the more wisdom flows out of you.
kurals.university: This is perhaps the most quoted kural of the chapter. It rests on a precise agricultural image from the Tamil landscape: the மணற்கேணி, a shallow well dug in sandy riverbed or soil, where groundwater seeps in more strongly the deeper one digs. The parallel verbs தொட்டனை ('as much as dug') and கற்றனை ('as much as learned') set up an exact proportion, and the shared verb ஊறும் ('springs, oozes up') links the two halves. The point is that wisdom (அறிவு, arivu) is not poured in from outside but springs up from within, released by the labour of study. It also implies that learning has no fixed end, since there is always more water below. Parallels range from Proverbs' 'wellspring of wisdom' and the Mishnah's 'ever-flowing spring' to Pope's 'Pierian spring'.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Taittiriya Upanishad, young Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him Brahman. Each time, he is told to go and practise tapas (disciplined inquiry). He comes to understand Brahman step by step as food, breath, mind, understanding, and finally bliss.
hinduism.explanation: Bhrigu's knowledge deepens in stages. Each round of effort 'digs' further and reveals a deeper layer of truth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's sand-well, understanding grows exactly as far as the seeker keeps digging through sustained effort.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the Bhrigu narrative. Knowledge deepening with effort is a good parallel, but there is no water or well image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs pictures wisdom as a spring that keeps flowing, deep water that wells up and never runs dry.
christianity.tie_back: A strong image match: both texts picture wisdom as water welling up from a deep source.
christianity._accuracy_note: Wording confirmed against multiple KJV sources. It shares the wellspring image, though not the 'proportional to digging' logic.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, “If the sea were ink for [writing] the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted, even if We brought the like of it in [continual] supplement.””
islam.explanation: The Qur'an uses an ocean image to show that divine knowledge has no limit. There is always more to learn.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's sand-well, it pictures knowledge as a water source that is never used up.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the Quran.com API. The inexhaustibility theme matches well. The 'more you dig, the more flows' logic is implicit rather than stated.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Eleazar ben Arach is like a spring that [ever] gathers force.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai praises his disciple as a spring whose flow keeps increasing, in contrast to another disciple who is 'a plastered cistern which loses not a drop' (retaining learning but not producing new insight).
judaism.tie_back: A striking parallel: the ideal scholar is an ever-growing spring, just as the Kural's learner is a well whose water rises with every bit of digging.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria. A spring image for a learned mind, closely matching the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Wisdom springs from meditation; without meditation wisdom wanes. Having known these two paths of progress and decline, let a man so conduct himself that his wisdom may increase.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that wisdom 'springs up' in proportion to cultivation and dries up when practice stops.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, wisdom rises in proportion to effort. Here the effort is meditation rather than study.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. The proportional-growth logic matches well. The practice named is meditation, not learning.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes the Muses of Mount Helicon bathing in the Hippocrene, the 'Horse's Spring' said to have been struck from the rock by Pegasus' hoof. Along with the Pierian spring, it became the classical symbol of the source of poetic and intellectual inspiration.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, wisdom and inspiration flow from sacred springs, and poets 'drink' from them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it pictures knowledge as water rising from a spring, though Greek myth stresses divine gift more than human digging.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. It shares the spring-of-knowledge image, but inspiration comes as a gift rather than from effort.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A little learning is a dang'rous thing; / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring: / There shallow draughts intoxicate the brain, / And drinking largely sobers us again.”
philosophy.explanation: Pope warns that shallow learning breeds arrogance, while deep learning brings sober wisdom. The depth of study decides the quality of understanding.
philosophy.tie_back: An excellent match: like Valluvar, Pope ties the benefit of learning to its depth, using the image of a spring.
philosophy.source: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism, Part II, lines 215–218 (1711)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Wording confirmed against Poetry Foundation and other editions. Depth-of-learning plus spring imagery is a close parallel.

kurals.tamil:
யாதானும் நாடாமால் ஊராமால் என்னொருவன்
சாந்துணையுங் கல்லாத வாறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Yaadhaanum naadaamaal ooraamaal ennoruvan
Saanthunaiyum kallaadha vaaru.
kurals.meaning: To a learned person, every country becomes their own country and every town their own town. So why would anyone go without learning, right up to the day they die?
kurals.elementary: A good doctor or teacher can move to any town and still be welcomed and needed. What you learn goes with you everywhere and makes you at home anywhere. So why would anyone ever stop learning?
kurals.university: The kural is built as a rhetorical question. Its premise is that for the learned, யாதானும் நாடாம், ஊராம் (any land is their land, any town is their town), because learning makes a person welcome and useful anywhere. Its conclusion asks why anyone would remain unlearned சாந்துணையும், 'even until death'. That phrase quietly adds the idea of lifelong learning: there is no age at which study becomes pointless. In the Porul section's concern with the practical world, this is an argument from utility. Land and local status can be lost, but learning is portable citizenship. The first idea matches the Sanskrit maxim that a scholar is honoured everywhere, and the second matches Solon's line about growing old while always learning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A well-known Sanskrit subhashita states: “svadeśe pūjyate rājā, vidvān sarvatra pūjyate”. A king is honoured in his own land, but a learned person is honoured everywhere.
hinduism.explanation: The proverb contrasts the local, limited honour of political power with the universal honour of learning.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-perfect match to the Kural's first half: the learned person is at home and respected in every land and town.
hinduism.source: Sanskrit subhashita (traditionally included in Chanakya Niti collections; attribution varies)
hinduism._accuracy_note: The widely cited Sanskrit wording is given with a translation, so it is marked as a paraphrase. Attribution and verse numbering differ between collections. A very close thematic match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.”
christianity.explanation: Daniel and his friends, exiles in a foreign empire, rise to high honour in the Babylonian court purely because of their learning and wisdom.
christianity.tie_back: A narrative example of the Kural's claim: through learning, the exile makes a foreign land his own.
christianity._accuracy_note: Wording confirmed against multiple KJV sources. A strong narrative parallel for learning being honoured abroad. The 'until death' element is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Joseph] said, “Appoint me over the storehouses of the land. Indeed, I will be a knowing guardian.””
islam.explanation: Joseph (Yusuf), sold as a slave into Egypt, becomes the trusted steward of a foreign kingdom because of his knowledge.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows knowledge turning a stranger's land into the place where he is honoured and entrusted.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified via the Quran.com API. A good narrative parallel. (The popular saying 'seek knowledge even unto China' was avoided because hadith scholars widely regard it as weak.)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Say not: ‘when I shall have leisure I shall study;’ perhaps you will not have leisure.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel warns against putting off study to a later time that may never come, since life is uncertain.
judaism.tie_back: This parallels the Kural's second half, its challenge to anyone who stays unlearned until death: do not postpone learning.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria. A strong match for the urgency of learning. The 'every land is his' element is absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better it is to live one day wise and meditative than to live a hundred years foolish and uncontrolled.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that a long life without wisdom is worth less than a single day lived wisely.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's rebuke of those who stay unlearned until death, it counts a lifetime without wisdom as wasted.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. A partial match: it values wisdom over length of life but does not mention being at home everywhere.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Odyssey opens by describing its hero as a man who saw the cities of many peoples and learned their minds.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus' defining trait is knowledge gained through wandering. It lets him survive, and even win honour, in one foreign land after another.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's learned person, Odysseus becomes a citizen of many cities through what he knows.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the proem, since translations vary. A good match for 'learning makes every land familiar'.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Solon, the Athenian lawgiver, is reported in Plato's Laches as saying that he grew old always learning many things. The Cynic Diogenes, asked where he came from, called himself 'a citizen of the world' (kosmopolitēs).
philosophy.explanation: Solon models lifelong learning right up to old age. Diogenes models the thinker whose home is the whole world rather than one city.
philosophy.tie_back: Together they cover both halves of the Kural: every land is the learned person's home, and learning should never stop until death.
philosophy.source: Plato, Laches 188b (Solon); Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.63 (Diogenes)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of two well-attested sayings. Combined, they closely match both lines of the Kural.

kurals.tamil:
ஒருமைக்கண் தான்கற்ற கல்வி ஒருவற்கு
எழுமையும் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Orumaikkan thaankatra kalvi oruvarku
Ezhumaiyum emaap pudaiththu.
kurals.meaning: The learning a person gains in one lifetime has the power to protect and help them through seven lifetimes to come.
kurals.elementary: Planting a tree helps you, your children and your grandchildren long after you have gone. Valluvar says learning is even bigger than that: what you learn now keeps helping you far into the future, even into future lives.
kurals.university: This kural draws on the Indian framework of rebirth. ஒருமை (orumai, 'one birth') is set against எழுமை (ezhumai, 'seven births'), a conventional expression for a long chain of future lives. The key word ஏமாப்பு (emaappu) means protection, security or support, so learning is pictured as a lasting safeguard that goes with the soul. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow the traditional rebirth reading. Kalaignar reinterprets it more secularly as learning that protects seven generations of a family. The kural fits the chapter's larger claim that learning, unlike other goods, is not used up or lost. Similar ideas appear in the Gita's teaching that a yogi's progress carries over into the next life and in Plato's theory that learning is recollection from earlier existence.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “On taking such a birth, he revives the divine consciousness of his previous life, and he again tries to make further progress in order to achieve complete success, O son of Kuru.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna assures Arjuna that spiritual progress and understanding are never lost at death. They carry into the next birth and continue from there.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-exact match to the Kural: what is gained in one life protects and advances a person in later lives.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Wording confirmed via vedabase.io search results. Carry-over of spiritual attainment across births directly parallels the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.”
christianity.explanation: Daniel's vision promises that the wise will shine for ever, so that their wisdom has an eternal result beyond this life.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the benefit of wisdom reaches past one lifetime. The framework is resurrection and eternity rather than rebirth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Standard KJV text. A moderate match: wisdom's lasting value beyond death, in a different eschatological frame.

islam.quote_or_event: “When a man dies, his acts come to an end, but three, recurring charity, or knowledge (by which people) benefit, or a pious child, who prays for him (for the deceased).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that beneficial knowledge is one of only three things that keep earning reward for a person after death.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats learning as one of the few goods whose benefit outlasts a single lifetime.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sunnah.com. A strong match for learning outlasting death, though in an afterlife frame rather than rebirth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For when a man passes away there accompany him neither gold nor silver, nor precious stones nor pearls, but Torah and good deeds alone.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yose ben Kisma refuses a fortune to live away from a place of learning, explaining that only Torah and good deeds go with a person beyond death.
judaism.tie_back: A very close match: learning is the possession that goes with a person past the end of this life.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria. It matches learning as a companion beyond death. Its frame is the world to come rather than seven births.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Buddhavamsa, the ascetic Sumedha resolves at the feet of the Buddha Dipankara to become a Buddha, then spends countless lives perfecting the paramis, including the perfection of wisdom (pañña). What he builds in each life carries forward to the next.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism teaches that cultivated wisdom and virtue are carried from life to life until they reach full Buddhahood.
buddhism.tie_back: A strong conceptual match: learning and wisdom gained in one birth protect and lift a person through many later births.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the traditional narrative. Its focus is spiritual perfections broadly rather than learning specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, souls choose their next lives. Plato's Socrates says the soul that has practised philosophy chooses wisely, while unphilosophical souls pick disastrous lives out of ignorance.
greek_mythology.explanation: Wisdom gained in one life shapes the quality of the next life a soul chooses.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, learning in one life gives protection across future lives.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A philosophical myth rather than traditional mythology, but a good rebirth-and-wisdom parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Meno, Socrates argues that the soul is immortal and has been born many times, so that what we call 'learning' is really recollection (anamnesis) of knowledge gained before.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, knowledge is carried across lives. The soul brings it into each new birth, and inquiry draws it out again.
philosophy.tie_back: A close conceptual parallel: learning is not confined to one lifetime but runs through many.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Plato's theory of recollection strikingly parallels the Kural's cross-life view of learning.

kurals.tamil:
தாமின் புறுவது உலகின் புறக்கண்டு
காமுறுவர் கற்றறிந் தார்.
kurals.meaning: When the learned see that the learning which delights them also delights the whole world, they come to love learning even more.
kurals.elementary: When you discover a great story and tell your friends, they love it too, and that makes you want to find even more stories. Learning works like that. Sharing it makes everyone happy, so you want to learn more.
kurals.university: The kural describes a self-reinforcing cycle of joy. The learned find pleasure (இன்புறுவது) in their own knowledge, then see that the same knowledge brings pleasure to the world (உலகு இன்புற). That discovery makes them desire (காமுறுவர்) learning all the more. Valluvar's use of kaamam, a word more often tied to love and desire, is striking: learning becomes a passion. The kural suggests that the highest motive for study is neither prestige nor profit but shared delight, which makes knowledge a social good. The idea is echoed in Seneca's statement that he learns only in order to teach, and in the Mishnah and hadith traditions that praise those who learn in order to share.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Gita describes the liberated sages as sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ, those who delight in the welfare of all beings, and says such people attain liberation.
hinduism.explanation: Krishna portrays the truly wise as people whose own inner fulfilment overflows into joyful work for the good of all living beings.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links the joy of the wise with the joy of the world. The Gita's focus is spiritual realization more than learning as such.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase built around the Sanskrit phrase. A moderate match: the wise delight in the world's good, but without the cycle of learning more.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples not to hide the light they have received, but to let it shine for the benefit of all.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats what one has received as something to share with the world. The Gospel does not describe the learner's growing desire for learning.
christianity._accuracy_note: Standard KJV text. A partial match on sharing one's light; the self-reinforcing love of learning is missing.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best among you (Muslims) are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet joins learning and teaching into a single excellence. The highest rank goes to those who both acquire knowledge and pass it on.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes learning and delighting others with it inseparable parts of one noble activity.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sunnah.com. A strong match for learning-to-share.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He who learns in order to teach, it is granted to him to study and to teach.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Ishmael teaches that someone who studies with the aim of sharing knowledge is rewarded with further opportunities to learn and to teach.
judaism.tie_back: A good match for the Kural's cycle: sharing learning leads to more learning.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria. The learn-teach-learn more cycle closely matches the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The gift of Dhamma excels all gifts; the taste of the Dhamma excels all tastes; the delight in Dhamma excels all delights.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls the sharing of true teaching the greatest gift and delight in the Dhamma the greatest delight.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it joins personal delight in wisdom with giving wisdom to others.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. Joy and gift in knowledge are both present, so this is a strong match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod sings of the Muses, whose songs gladden the great mind of Zeus. When a person loved by the Muses sings, people weighed down with grief forget their sorrows.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, the gifts of the Muses (poetry, song and learning) delight both gods and humans and relieve the world's sorrow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows learning and art spreading joy outward to the whole world.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A good match for learning as shared delight; the learner's growing desire for more is not explicit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Lucilius that he is glad to learn so that he may teach. No knowledge, however excellent, would please him if he had to keep it to himself, and he would refuse wisdom itself if it came on condition of never sharing it.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, the joy of learning cannot be separated from the joy of sharing it. Knowledge kept to oneself loses its pleasure.
philosophy.tie_back: An excellent match: the learner's delight grows through the delight of others, which is the Kural's exact cycle.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 6.4
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close paraphrase of the Gummere translation. It is not presented verbatim because the exact wording could not be fully confirmed. A very close thematic match.

kurals.tamil:
கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி யொருவற்கு
மாடல்ல மற்றை யவை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kedil vizhuchchelvam kalvi oruvarku
Maadalla matraiyavai.
kurals.meaning: Learning is the one excellent wealth that can never be destroyed. Compared with it, all other possessions are not true wealth at all.
kurals.elementary: Toys can break, money can be lost, and a house can burn down. What you have learned stays in your head, and no one can steal it. That is why Valluvar calls learning the best treasure of all.
kurals.university: The chapter ends with its thesis. Learning is கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம், 'imperishable, excellent wealth', and all other things are மாடு அல்ல, 'not wealth'. மாடு (maadu) is an old Tamil word for wealth that originally meant cattle, the earliest form of property, which gives the claim an archaic force. The argument works on two levels. Materially, learning cannot be stolen, taxed, destroyed or divided. Evaluatively, only learning deserves the name 'wealth' at all. Placing this conclusion in the Porul (Wealth) section is pointed, since Valluvar redefines the very wealth that section is about. The same claim appears almost word for word in the Sanskrit verse on vidyā-dhana, the wealth of knowledge that thieves cannot steal and kings cannot seize.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A famous Sanskrit subhashita says: “na cora-hāryaṃ na ca rāja-hāryaṃ na bhrātṛ-bhājyaṃ na ca bhāra-kāri; vyaye kṛte vardhata eva nityaṃ vidyā-dhanaṃ sarva-dhana-pradhānam.” Thieves cannot steal it, kings cannot seize it, brothers cannot divide it, and it is no burden to carry. When spent, it only grows. The wealth of knowledge is the foremost of all wealth.
hinduism.explanation: The verse lists every way ordinary wealth can be lost and shows that none of them applies to learning.
hinduism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: learning is imperishable wealth, and it is the chief of all wealth.
hinduism.source: Traditional Sanskrit subhashita on vidyā-dhana (widely cited; exact textual origin uncertain)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Widely cited Sanskrit wording with a translation, marked as a paraphrase because translations vary and the original anthology source is uncertain. A near-identical theme.

christianity.quote_or_event: “How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs ranks wisdom and understanding far above precious metals as the truly valuable possession.
christianity.tie_back: A strong match: learning outranks material wealth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Standard KJV text. It directly ranks wisdom above wealth; the 'imperishable' point is implicit.

islam.quote_or_event: “The learned are the heirs of the Prophets, and the Prophets leave neither dinar nor dirham, leaving only knowledge, and he who takes it takes an abundant portion.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that the real inheritance of the prophets is knowledge, not money, and that whoever gains it has received a rich share.
islam.tie_back: An excellent match: knowledge is the true wealth, and coins are not the inheritance worth having.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 3641 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sunnah.com. It directly contrasts knowledge with money as the true inheritance.

judaism.quote_or_event: Midrash Tanchuma tells of a scholar on a ship full of merchants. They mock him for carrying no goods, and he says his merchandise is greater than theirs. Pirates seize everything the merchants own. When they land, the destitute merchants are ignored, while the scholar is welcomed and honoured by the townspeople for his learning.
judaism.explanation: The story shows in narrative form that learning is the one possession pirates cannot take and the one that provides for its owner anywhere.
judaism.tie_back: A perfect narrative parallel: all other wealth disappears, and learning alone remains indestructible and valuable.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the midrash, confirmed via Sefaria and Chabad.org retellings. A near-exact thematic match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Nidhikanda Sutta contrasts treasure buried in the ground, which can be lost, stolen or forgotten, with a 'treasure' of generosity, virtue, restraint and self-control. That inner treasure goes with its owner, cannot be taken by others, and cannot be stolen by thieves.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines real treasure as inner qualities that no loss can touch.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares ordinary wealth perishable and inner wealth imperishable. Its treasure is merit and virtue rather than learning as such.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A strong structural match for imperishable versus perishable wealth, but its 'treasure' is merit rather than learning. The source page could not be fetched during this session because of a rate limit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asks Dionysus that everything he touches should turn to gold. When even his food and drink turn to metal, he begs to be freed from the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows that material wealth, however great, cannot sustain life and may even destroy it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It supports the negative half of the Kural: other possessions are not true wealth. It says nothing directly about learning.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak to moderate match. It is a cautionary tale about the emptiness of material wealth, with no counterpart about learning.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells of the philosopher Stilpo. His city was captured and he lost his wife, children and property, yet when the conqueror asked whether he had lost anything, he answered that all his goods were with him, meaning his wisdom and virtue.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoics, the only true possessions are those of the mind, which no conqueror can take.
philosophy.tie_back: An excellent match: everything else can be lost, but the wealth of the mind is imperishable and alone deserves to be called wealth.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 9.18–19
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Seneca's anecdote (the saying is often rendered 'omnia mea mecum sunt'). A close parallel.
